item.text:
Yes—hERG/IKr liability is a defining pharmacology of sotalol, and I would treat the ToxPred call as a false negative.

Sotalol is a Vaughan Williams class III antiarrhythmic that directly inhibits hERG/Kv11.1-mediated IKr. The block is state/protocol dependent and relatively low-affinity compared with agents such as dofetilide, which can make it difficult for some binary models or screening protocols to classify correctly. Direct experiments have nevertheless demonstrated substantial hERG-current inhibition by d-sotalol under repetitive depolarization. [Numaguchi et al., *Circulation Research*](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11090546/)

More importantly, the clinical signal is unequivocal: sotalol produces dose- and concentration-related QT/QTc prolongation and can cause torsade de pointes. The US label carries a boxed warning for life-threatening proarrhythmia and requires ECG monitoring and renal-function-based dosing. Risk increases with renal impairment, higher exposure, bradycardia, hypokalaemia/hypomagnesaemia, female sex, and heart failure. [FDA prescribing information](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2023/019865Orig1s026Corrected_lbl.pdf)

Regarding this prediction:

- The blocker score, 0.314 versus a 0.413 threshold, is not far below the model cutoff and is not a probability of clinical safety.
- The applicability check only confirms familiar elements; it provides no structural-neighbourhood support because `similarity_domain` is null.
- The negative Tox21 calls do not mitigate the electrophysiology risk; those assays address different mechanisms.
- The submitted SMILES is stereochemically unspecified. Commercial sotalol is racemic; both enantiomers have class III activity, whereas most beta-blockade comes from the l-enantiomer.

For the project team, I would annotate sotalol as a **known hERG/IKr-positive, QT-prolonging, torsadogenic clinical comparator** and exclude this model result from any weight-of-evidence “negative” count. It is useful as a translational QT/proarrhythmia comparator, but because its direct hERG potency is protocol-sensitive and comparatively weak, I would pair it with a potent assay-control blocker such as dofetilide or E-4031. Confirm concentration–response under a validated physiological-temperature patch-clamp protocol and, if needed, add an integrated repolarization assay such as human ventricular tissue or hiPSC-cardiomyocyte APD/EAD measurements.
